body_paragraphs: Trump says a Hormuz deal is 'imminent' and that Gulf allies asked him to hold off strikes over the weekend; Tehran's own media denies asking for that holdoff and denies agreeing to split control of the strait. Oil slipped anyway on the optimism. Five months in, the gap between the announcement and the confirmation remains the whole story.

Otto Lopez's market thinned overnight - Boston's talks with Miami are reportedly dead over asking price - with the trade deadline landing at 6pm tonight and his fate still open. Markets reopen after a weekend of prediction-market noise: September hike odds anywhere from the mid-50s to mid-60s depending which platform you trust, ahead of Friday's jobs report.

Locally, two things you starred yesterday both moved: early voting opened this morning on Marine Stadium's restoration referendum, and Miami's office rents set yet another citywide record, this time by a second data provider's count. Tonight's reading leans away from the news cycle - a lost Amazonian civilization visible only from the air, and the Veneto-style villa James Deering built on Biscayne Bay a century ago.

Three stars came in from you yesterday - Marine Stadium, the Marlins, and Miami's office market - all reflected in today's edition. But for a second morning running, this run couldn't reach your private notes or long-term memory, so none of that could actually be learned from or carried forward. Worth knowing if that connection matters to you.

themes.title: Trump calls a Hormuz deal 'imminent' - Iran's own media denies asking for the holdoff or agreeing to split the strait
themes.thesis: A day after Trump said he'd cancelled strikes over an agreed framework, Iran's media directly disputes the specifics of that framework, even as both sides say talks resume today.
themes.synthesis: Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that a Hormuz deal is 'imminent,' with negotiations set to resume Monday, and repeated his claim that Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, and other regional powers asked him to hold off on planned weekend strikes. Iranian semi-official media pushed back harder than Sunday's vaguer non-confirmation: it explicitly denied that Iran had asked for any holdoff, and separately denied agreeing to any arrangement that would split control of the strait. In a second, distinct thread, Iran's foreign minister said negotiations with Oman over a new maritime shipping route through Hormuz are in 'final stages' - but Iran's foreign ministry spokesman was careful to note that this Oman-brokered mechanism has nothing to do with whether the strait itself reopens to normal traffic. Oil prices eased Monday on deal optimism regardless of Iran's denials, though tankers reportedly continue to face attacks and are being forced to turn back.
themes.new_today: Iran's explicit denial of the holdoff request and the strait-splitting claim, the distinct Oman route talks reaching 'final stages,' and Monday's oil price move.
themes.why_it_matters: This is a more specific rebuttal than Sunday's silence - not just a failure to confirm, but a direct contradiction of Trump's account - which matters for anyone reading oil and rate exposure off the war's day-to-day headlines rather than its actual resolution.

themes.title: LiDAR finds a civilization of millions hiding under the Amazon canopy for over a thousand years
themes.thesis: Airborne laser scanning just found more than 400 well-preserved archaeological sites belonging to a multicultural Amazonian civilization nobody had properly mapped - proof the 'pristine wilderness' framing of the Amazon was always partly wrong.
themes.synthesis: Researchers using airborne laser scanning (LiDAR) identified more than 400 well-preserved archaeological sites tied to the Aquiry civilization, which flourished in southwestern Amazonia between roughly 600 BCE and 850 CE across an estimated 183,000 square kilometers. The detected features - geometric earthworks, straight roads, and ceremonial centers - suggest the fuller territory could contain more than 20,000 ancient ceremonial centers, with a population that may have reached 1.2 to 3 million people at its height. The findings reframe large stretches of the Amazon as a heavily engineered landscape shaped by human hands for centuries, not the untouched wilderness it's often imagined to be.
themes.new_today: First dedicated coverage of the 400-site LiDAR survey and its territory-wide population and earthwork estimates in this edition.
themes.why_it_matters: Appreciation-worthy with zero urgency attached - a genuine counterweight after a morning of trade deadlines and disputed ceasefires, and a reminder that scale itself can hide in plain sight for over a thousand years.

themes.title: The Veneto villa James Deering built on Biscayne Bay, a century before anyone called Miami a capital market
themes.thesis: A century before institutional capital started chasing Miami real estate, one industrialist's winter home already argued that the bay was worth building something extraordinary on.
themes.synthesis: James Deering's Vizcaya, built between 1914 and 1922 in Coconut Grove, reworked the eighteenth-century country villas of Italy's Veneto region for a subtropical bayfront, with architect F. Burrall Hoffman and design director Paul Chalfin adapting Mediterranean Revival and Italian Renaissance forms to Florida's climate. The Main House holds 34 decorated rooms surrounded by ten acres of formal gardens, filled with European antiquities and American art commissioned specifically for the estate. It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1994, one of the most intact surviving examples of the era when America's newly wealthy built European-style estates at home rather than abroad.
themes.new_today: First dedicated coverage of Vizcaya's construction history in this edition, as background to tonight's beautiful thing.
themes.why_it_matters: A quiet counterweight to a morning of deadlines and disputed ceasefires - proof that Biscayne Bay has been worth serious ambition for a hundred years, long before this week's rent records.

daily_puzzle.prompt: Three neighbors - Ana, Ben, and Cleo - are asked who left the shared gate open overnight. Ana says: 'Ben is lying.' Ben says: 'Cleo is lying.' Cleo says: 'Ana and Ben are both lying.' Exactly one of the three is telling the truth. Who is it?
daily_puzzle.hint: Assume each one is truthful in turn and check whether that assumption survives contact with all three statements.
daily_puzzle.explanation: If Ben is truthful, Cleo is lying - which makes Cleo's claim ('both Ana and Ben are lying') false, consistent since Ben isn't lying. That forces Ana's statement ('Ben is lying') to be false too, so Ana lies - exactly one truth-teller, as required. Starting from Ana or Cleo instead produces zero or two truth-tellers, both ruled out by the setup.

US carries out no new strikes overnight for the first time since the ceasefire collapsed; an Omani delegation arrives in Tehran to discuss Strait of Hormuz shipping; Brent eases to about $96.80, down nearly 4% but still up over 12% on the week.

The pause holds through the weekend into Monday with no new strikes reported on either front; Brent tumbles toward the mid-$80s, down roughly 7% on the session, as Trump signals openness to renewed talks with Tehran.

Trump and Netanyahu meet at the White House for the first time since the war began, calling the talks 'positive and productive' and reaffirming a shared commitment against an Iranian nuclear weapon; Brent eases further into the mid-to-high $80s.

The US launches a 'heavy wave' of new strikes on Iran; Iranian state media reports at least three civilians killed. Iran retaliates against Jordan and Kuwait, killing a worker at a Chinese-owned building in Kuwait. Trump says it is now 'our turn' to hit Iran hard.
Qatar formally condemns Iran's strikes on Jordan and Kuwait as violations of sovereignty - the first significant regional diplomatic reaction against Tehran this round.

Iran's army claims strikes on US assets at Kuwait's Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base and Bahrain's Sheikh Isa Air Base; neither government confirms it. The US conducts no fresh strikes overnight - the first pause since Wednesday's heavy wave.

Egypt reports a drone of unknown origin hit two gas vessels at its Damietta port, a possible first sign the conflict is pulling in a new country; Brent eases 1.4% to $87.78 as Hormuz tanker traffic shows tentative recovery.

Kuwait's army confirms it intercepted a fresh wave of Iranian drones aimed at a government facility and civilian vehicles, the attack Iran claimed Thursday and nobody had confirmed. A tanker is hit by an unidentified projectile near Oman.

At Camp David, Trump says the US is planning new strikes on Iran 'as soon as this weekend'; only 28% of Americans approve of his handling of the five-month-old war. Brent back above $90, WTI near $84.67.
Trump says he's cancelled the planned strikes, citing an agreed framework on reopening the Strait of Hormuz after MBS and other regional leaders pressed for de-escalation over the weekend.

Iranian state media gives no sign it agrees to any deal; Fars news agency calls Trump's terms a 'wish list' and Iran's foreign ministry warns of a 'decisive response' to any future US-Israeli aggression.

threads.title: 2026 CRE capital markets under pressure
threads.current_state: South Florida commercial sales volume remains down 13% year over year, and the summer's biggest single industrial deal - Waste Management's $379M purchase of 146 acres in Medley - was 96% seller-financed. Rents in Miami's most sought-after office towers broke $200/sqft in July, anchored by Peter Thiel's family office paying a record $250/sqft at 830 Brickell. Two independent data sets now confirm the citywide trend: TenantBase puts the full-service asking rent at an all-time high of $63.63/sqft, and Commercial Observer separately puts the average at $67.12/sqft (+7% YoY) - both pointing the same direction even as exact figures vary $59.66-67.12/sqft depending on methodology.

timeline.summary: First tracked: CBRE Q2 update shows deal volume down 24% YoY, construction spending below plan, hiring slowing.
South Florida-specific data surfaces: commercial sales volume down 13% year over year to $5.42B in H1 2026.
Waste Management pays $379M for 146 acres in Medley to build a landfill; $366M of the price, 96%, is seller financing rather than a bank loan.

A LoopNet analysis of roughly 5,000 office listings finds Miami's average asking rent, $59.66/sq ft, now the highest in the US, ahead of New York's $50.56 - a sign of how much capital has relocated to Miami since 2020 even as deal volume overall stays soft.

Pebb Capital buys a Miami Beach office building with $69M in ACORE Capital financing; a Wynwood commercial parcel sells for $24.5M, the region's priciest trade that week - real transactions behind the aggregate rent data.
Rents in Miami's top towers cross $200/sqft for the first time, anchored by Peter Thiel's family office paying a record $250/sqft at 830 Brickell; Q2 leasing citywide up nearly 45% YoY to 1.3M sq ft.
Citywide full-service asking rent hits an all-time high of $63.63/sqft (+2.0% QoQ, +6.3% YoY), with 429,712 sqft of positive Q2 absorption.

A separate Commercial Observer analysis puts Miami's average asking rent at $67.12/sqft, up 7% year over year, with availability down to 14.9% from 17.1% - an independent data set reinforcing the same trend TenantBase reported yesterday.

threads.title: Miami Marine Stadium's restoration referendum
threads.current_state: Early voting is open, running through August 16, ahead of the August 18 vote on Referendum #172, a 40-year management deal with Global Spectrum/Oak View Group and local partner Breakwater Hospitality. Under the deal, the city keeps 93% of event revenue and 85% of sponsorship income, with up to $10M toward restoration up front, followed by a separate $65-85M restoration bond. Partial pile and seating repairs are already underway with county and state grant money.

timeline.summary: First tracked: City Commission approved the Global Spectrum/Oak View management deal in February; referendum set for August 18; partial restoration already underway.

Additional detail surfaces: the deal is formally Referendum #172, with early voting set for August 3-16 and a specified revenue split (93% events, 85% sponsorship) plus a separate $65-85M restoration bond beyond the initial $10M.
Early voting confirmed to begin tomorrow, August 3; the adjacent Seaquarium site's marina redevelopment surfaces as a related but separate decision over the same stretch of public waterfront.
Early voting opens as scheduled, running through August 16 ahead of the August 18 vote.

threads.title: Miami Seaquarium's marina redevelopment
threads.current_state: Miami-Dade County and Terra Group/David Martin have applied to build what could be the county's largest marina at the shuttered Seaquarium site on Virginia Key - 325 slips (about 90 for yachts over 80ft), a 500-boat dry stack, a fuel depot, and floating docks extending partway across the channel. Environmental regulators have raised concerns about wetlands, coral, and water quality; if approved, demolition could start late 2026 with an opening target around 2029. Martin bought the Seaquarium's lease for $22.5M after the park closed in October 2025 after 70 years, and plans to keep an aquarium plus add a Fishermen's Village-style restaurant district and public baywalk.

timeline.summary: First tracked: marina application details surface - 325 slips, 500-boat dry stack, fuel depot; environmental review pending; potential late-2026 groundbreaking.
